lessonTitle: Relative risk, odds ratio and hazard ratio

slides.title: RR, OR and HR Are Not Interchangeable
bullets: Relative risk, odds ratio and hazard ratio all compare event occurrence between two groups
Each measure fits a different study design
Confusing them is one of the most common interpretation errors, even among experienced clinicians

slides.title: The Ratio of Two Probabilities
bullets: Relative risk compares the probability of an event in the treated group versus the control group
Used in trials and cohort studies, where incidence can be calculated directly
An RR of 0.70 means a 30% lower relative risk of the event in the treated group

slides.title: The Measure for Case-Control Studies
bullets: Odds ratio compares the odds of the event between groups, not a directly calculated incidence
It's the standard measure in case-control studies, where true incidence can't be computed
When the event is rare, below roughly 10%, the OR closely approximates the RR
When the event is common, the OR tends to exaggerate the effect size

slides.title: The Measure for Time-to-Event Data
bullets: Hazard ratio is used in survival analysis, when the timing of the event matters, not just whether it happens
It reflects relative instantaneous risk over follow-up, assuming proportional hazards
It's the standard measure in oncology and cardiovascular trials

slides.title: A Favorable Ratio Can Hide a Small Absolute Benefit

stats.label: sounds highly favorable on its own
the same result when the event is rare

slides.caption: None of these three measures show the real absolute benefit for an individual patient.

slides.title: Never Report a Relative Measure Alone
bullets: None of these measures communicate absolute risk or the real magnitude of benefit
Pair every relative measure with the absolute risk in each group
Add the number needed to treat to translate the effect into practice-ready language

takeaway.title: RR, OR and HR each fit a different design, and none show absolute benefit alone
bullets: Relative risk fits trials and cohorts, odds ratio fits case-control studies, hazard ratio fits time-to-event data
A favorable relative number can still hide a small absolute benefit
Always pair a relative measure with absolute risk before discussing it with an HCP
